oracles.rationale:
🫥️ RECLASSIFIED. The third-party crate here does REAL codec work — it decodes the artifact and will reject a malformed one — but that is not what the mutation test turns on. What the OUTPUT OF A MUTATION SHOULD BE is computed by this owner's own `🦀️oracle.rs`, whose `apply_kind` dispatch is a second implementation of this subset's mutation semantics. Its own doc comment says so: it "deliberately mirrors" the production `diff` rather than diverging from it. Both halves of the comparison therefore read the same specification, and a misreading of it produces two agreeing wrong answers.

The honest split is that the crate discharges "the result is a well-formed file of this format", and NOT "the mutation computed the right answer". Only the second is what a mutation oracle is for, so this is a `cross-semio-implementation`: a required SUPPLEMENT, never a substitute. A qualifying third-party reference for the mutation semantics is still owed.

productionDebt.plan: The `image` crate is production-reachable TODAY from two places: the 🎞️animate plugin's video engine and 🧰️framework/🔨️modules/🗺️surface's tiled-map. Discovered by the oracle-purity gate the moment `image` was registered — the gate did its job. Phase 7 target: both call sites want raster decode/encode that ✏️s/🔌️plugins/🗄️stdio already implements, so routing them through decode_bmp / decode_tiff / decode_jpg retires the dependency and this record with it.

oracles.rationale:
📖️ A READER, and that is the whole point of registering it separately.

This subset also carries a `🦀️oracle.rs` that COMPUTES what each mutation should produce (registered above as `image-tiff-6-0-mutate`, `cross-semio-implementation`). That entry does not discharge anything on its own, because both halves of such a comparison descend from one reading of the specification.

This entry is a different mechanism. The expected state is not computed at all — it is COMMITTED, as the `after` half of a byte-reproducible fixture (`../🧫️fixtures/`). `tiff` 0.11.3 then parses the whole IFD chain on BOTH sides — via its own `Decoder::{more_images,next_image,tag_iter,byte_order}` — and the comparison is over what it recovered. The probes say so in their own header: "Everything here MARSHALS and READS; nothing here applies a mutation or predicts what one should."

So the judge is a third-party implementation of the format, and nothing in this repository predicts the answer it is judging. That is what makes it qualifying where the sibling entry is not.

🔎️ `package`/`version` name the crate this session's own investigation determined actually carries the structural visibility this catalog needs: `image` 0.25's public TIFF surface (`image::codecs::tiff::{TiffEncoder,TiffDecoder}`, confirmed by reading the vendored crate source) is single-IFD-only with no tag/byte-order accessors — it cannot witness `insert-ifd`/`remove-ifd`/`replace-tag`/`remove-tag` at all. `tiff` 0.11.3 is the lower-level crate `image` itself uses for TIFF (same composition shape this repository's own `avi`/`bcf` oracles already use — a lower, more generic crate composed for real structural visibility), and its `Decoder`/`TiffEncoder` give full multi-IFD chain navigation, whole-IFD tag enumeration (including an `unknown(u16)` tag variant for non-baseline tags) and the file byte-order mark directly. `image` is therefore not a dependency of this oracle's codec at all — see `../🏭️generator/🦀️tiff-ifd-codec/src/main.rs`'s own header for the full investigation trail.

⚠️ `change-byte-order` is EXCLUDED from this oracle's witnessed set for a different, sharper reason than the other kinds' generic reader-visibility question: `tiff` 0.11.3's ENCODER hardcodes the byte-order mark to the compiling target's native endianness at compile time (`#[cfg(target_endian="little"|"big")]` in its own `src/encoder/writer.rs`), never runtime-selectable. Every platform this entry is registered for above is little-endian, so this library cannot WRITE a big-endian `after.tiff` fixture on any of them — not a reader-visibility gap but a writer-side platform lock discovered by trying. See `../🔣️oracle.json`'s own `mutationManifests` entry for `change-byte-order` (capability renamed `tiff-6-0-mutate-uncarried`) and this ticket's own `📓️tiff-6-0-document-reader-oracle-retrofit.md` for the full reasoning and the refused build's own captured stderr.

🧭️ `productionReachable: false` here is a DELIBERATE narrower claim than the sibling `image-tiff-6-0-mutate` entry's own `productionReachable: true` above (with its `productionDebt` block naming two real call sites). Both can be true at once: grepping every non-test, non-oracle `Cargo.toml` that declares `image` as a real dependency (`✏️s/🔌️plugins/🎞️animate`, `✏️s/🔌️plugins/🖍️draw`, `🧰️framework/🔨️modules/🗺️surface`, `🧰️framework/🛍️products/💻️os/🔨️modules/♾️infinite`, `.../📺️renderer/…/🎯️targets/🧊️wgpu`) shows every one of them enables only `["png", "jpeg", "webp", "gif"]`-shaped feature sets — none enables `image`'s `tiff` feature, and none imports `image::codecs::tiff` or decodes TIFF bytes anywhere in their own source (confirmed by reading `✏️s/🔌️plugins/🎞️animate/…/🎥️video/🦀️.rs` and `🧰️framework/🔨️modules/🗺️surface/🗺️tiled-map/🦀️.rs` directly — both use `image` only for PNG/RGBA buffers). So `image` the crate is production-reachable for OTHER formats, but `image`'s TIFF support specifically is not — and this entry depends on `tiff` directly, not `image`, which is not production-reachable from anywhere in this repository at all.

📖️ The declared BYTE ORDER, which no pixel-level projection can see — the crate says so itself: `byte_order()` is documented as "only relevant to interpreting raw bytes read from tags", because "the image decoding methods will correct to the host byte order automatically". This subset's other reader projects decoded pixels, so `change-byte-order` was invisible to it.

This ticket recorded the kind as writer-blocked TWICE, on two real but narrow measurements: `tiff` 0.11's encoder rejects a non-native order with `UsageError::ByteOrderMismatch`, and Pillow's `im.save(..., format='TIFF')` emits `II` regardless of any prefix hint. Both hold. What neither covered is Pillow's own IFD SERIALISER: `ImageFileDirectory_v2(ifh=b'MM\x00\x2a...')` encodes every tag in the requested endianness, so the library does the field layout and the generator only lays out the 8-byte header and concatenates the strip. Nothing hand-encodes a TIFF field.

The projection carries the pixel CHECKSUM beside the order, and the generator refuses a pair whose checksums differ: a `change-byte-order` fixture must differ in the order and in nothing else, and one that also moved the image would pass a bare order comparison while proving less than it appears to. Measured: both files decode to checksum 2464.

qualification.evidence: Validated BOTH ways this session with real measured numbers: replace-tag-applied's before.tiff vs before.tiff (byte-identical pair) -> {equal:true, diffCount:0}; replace-tag-applied's before.tiff vs after.tiff (one tag's value deliberately changed) -> {equal:false, diffCount:1, diffs:["$.ifds[0].entries[5].value.value: \"original scan\" \u2260 \"rescanned copy\""]}.

qualification.evidence: Validated BOTH ways: (before,before) -> equal:true; (before,after) -> equal:false, on LittleEndian -> BigEndian. The same 8x8 image written twice through Pillow's own IFD serialiser, once little-endian and once big-endian. Both decode to an identical pixel checksum, so the pair differs in the declared byte order and in nothing else — checked at generation time. tiff 0.11 corrects to host order during image decoding, so only Decoder::byte_order() witnesses this.

comparisonProfiles.description: The declared byte order, plus dimensions, colour type, sample count and a pixel checksum — the last so that a pair claiming to change only the order can be shown to change only the order.
